content.title: About
content.content: Christophine (also known as black cucumber or African eggplant) is an edible fruit of a tropical plant in the gourd family. When cooked it becomes tender, slightly sweet, and has a soft texture. In cuisine it is commonly used in soups, stews, and braised dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Christophine originates from Africa but is now cultivated in tropical regions of Asia and South America.
The fruit contains a few small seeds that resemble tiny pumpkin seeds.
Unlike common eggplant, christophine has a thicker skin that holds its shape during long cooking.
Traditionally it is featured in curry dishes and Indian "saag" preparations.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked christophine retains a notable amount of vitamin C, which supports immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other gourds, christophine is low in fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic compounds in christophine may help reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to gourds, including christophine.

items.title: Beware of unripe fruit
items.content: Unripe christophine can contain higher levels of bitter compounds that may irritate the stomach.

items.title: Nutrient interactions
items.content: Large amounts may interfere with the absorption of certain minerals such as iron.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook christophine until tender, then add it to soups, stews, curries, or use it as a filling for pies. It can also be diced and tossed into vegetable salads after cooling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked christophine in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags.
